q: You draw a straight line on the Mercator chart from your departure to the next waypoint and read its direction off the rose. If you steer that true course, what track do you follow?
a: A rhumb line — one true course all the way
o: A great circle — the shortest way on the globe
A curve that bends towards the pole
A line whose course changes at each meridian
why: Mercator keeps angles true: a straight line on it is a rhumb line, crossing every meridian at the same angle.

q: You are measuring a leg near the top of this small-scale passage chart. Where do you read the miles?
a: On the latitude scale level with the leg
o: On the latitude scale at the bottom edge
On the longitude scale along the top edge
On any part of the latitude scale
why: On a Mercator chart the latitude scale stretches towards the pole; read the miles level with the leg's own latitude.

q: You span the leg A–B with the dividers and carry them to the chart's borders. How long is the leg?
why: Distance is read on the latitude scale: 1' of latitude = 1 M, so 19.5' − 12.0' = 7.5 M. Longitude minutes shrink with latitude.

fig.title: Leg A–B on the chart
lines: Dividers on the latitude scale beside
Same span on the longitude scale: 11.7'

q: You are closing an unfamiliar harbour entrance with rocky ledges either side. Which chart do you navigate on now?
a: Chart B — larger scale, more detail
o: Chart A — it shows the whole picture
Either — both show the same dangers
Chart A — a smaller scale is more exact
why: Use the largest-scale chart of the area: 1:25,000 shows dangers, marks and soundings that 1:150,000 leaves out.

fig.title: Charts aboard
lines: Now: closing an entrance between ledges

q: You plot a fix on this passage chart close to the coast. How much ground does a 1 mm slip of the pencil cover?
a: About 200 m
o: About 20 m
About 2 km
About 2 M
why: 1 mm × 200,000 = 200 m, about a cable — too coarse near a danger. Move to a larger-scale chart.

fig.title: Plotting a fix
lines: Your pencil point: about 1 mm wide

q: You need this buoy's position for your waypoint list. What do you write down?
why: Latitude: 0.9' south of 50°20'N = 50°19.1'N. Longitude: 3.0' east of 004°10'W = 004°07.0'W — west longitude falls eastward.

fig.note: Parallels and meridians from the border

q: Your crew reads the GPS position aloud: 50°18.5'N 004°06.0'W. Which mark on the chart is the boat?
a: C
o: A
B
D
why: 50°18.5'N is 1.5' south of 50°20'N; 004°06.0'W is 4' east of 004°10'W. The two meet at C.

fig.note: Parallels and meridians from the border

q: The next waypoint lies on your own parallel. How far away is it, and in which direction?
a: 3.2 M to the west
o: 5.0 M to the west
3.2 M to the east
5.0 M to the east
why: West longitude grows westward. 5' of longitude at 50°20'N = 5 × cos 50.3° ≈ 3.2 M — measure it on the latitude scale.

q: Your crew plots the handheld GPS position on the chart, whose scales are in minutes and decimals. How far out is the plot?
a: About 3 cables, too far south
o: About 3 cables, too far north
About 30 m — it does not matter
About 3 M, too far south
why: 45" = 0.75', not 0.45': the plot is 0.30' of latitude (0.3 M) too far south; 12" = 0.20' adds only 0.08' of longitude.

q: Your GPS and plotter are set to WGS84. What do you do to a GPS position before plotting it on this paper chart?
a: Nothing — plot it as it is
o: Apply a datum shift north and east
Add the height of tide to it
Convert it to a local datum first
why: The chart is on WGS84, the same datum as the GPS, so its latitude and longitude plot directly.

fig.title: Chart title panel
lines: Depths in metres below chart datum

q: You are approaching the Galician coast on this older chart. Which position do you plot for the GPS reading?
why: Northward adds to N latitude: 27.30' + 0.06' = 27.36'. Eastward takes away from W longitude: 16.40' − 0.09' = 16.31'.

fig.title: Note on the chart
lines: and 0.09' EAST to agree with this chart

q: The plotter draws the boat on the breakwater while you are clearly in the fairway. What is the most likely cause?
a: The GPS datum does not match the chart
o: The compass needs a new deviation card
The tidal stream has set you sideways
The GPS antenna is mounted too high
why: A GPS set to ED50 feeding a WGS84 chart shifts the boat 100 m or more. Set the GPS to the chart's datum.

fig.title: Entering the marina at dusk
lines: Plotter: boat drawn on the breakwater
You: mid-fairway, leading lights in line
GPS set-up menu: map datum ED50

q: You are approaching this Aegean islet at night, steering by the plotter. What do you do?
a: Pass far wider than the 0.3' offset
o: Trust the plotter — GPS is good to 10 m
Shift every GPS fix 0.3' to the north
Keep the track — 0.2 M is two cables
why: An unknown offset of up to 0.3' (about 550 m) is bigger than the 0.2 M gap. Pass far wider; check by eye, depth and radar.

fig.title: Night approach to an islet
lines: Chart from an old survey; its note:
by up to 0.3'; offset not known'
Plotter: reef 0.2 M off your track

q: You plan to enter this harbour tonight. What do you make of the chart?
a: Out of date — get a current edition
o: Fine — coastlines and depths seldom change
Fine — the edition is only a print date
Fine at night — the lights are unchanged
why: An old edition with no corrections misses the new breakwater and buoys. Navigate on a current, corrected chart.

q: You find this old chart of a Greek bay aboard and plan to anchor on the charted 3. What depth do you expect at chart datum?
a: About 5.5 m
o: About 3.0 m
About 0.9 m
About 1.6 m
why: Read the units in the title: 3 fathoms × 1.83 m = 5.5 m. Fathom and metric charts look alike at a glance.

q: You are passing these three rocks at high water springs. Which one will you still see above the surface?
a: A — it stands 2.5 m above MHWS
o: B — it dries 1.2 m above datum
C — it has a depth printed by it
None — every rock covers at HW
why: A figure in brackets is a height above MHWS, so A stays dry. B's underlined 1.2 dries only near LW; C has 4.3 m over it.

q: Your passage plan runs straight over this wreck. What do you do?
a: Replan to pass outside the dotted line
o: Keep the track — 18 m all round is ample
Keep the track, but only near high water
Keep the track — wrecks are a ship's worry
why: A wreck inside a dotted danger line with no depth is dangerous to surface navigation: keep outside the line.

fig.title: On your planned track
lines: Wreck symbol inside a dotted line

q: Your track runs over the obstruction on the chart. What do you do?
a: Alter round it — too little water
o: Carry on — 9 m all round it
Carry on — 2.2 m clears a 2.1 m keel
Carry on — obstructions are swept
why: Obstn 1.8 is a least depth of 1.8 m. With 0.4 m of tide that is 2.2 m — 0.1 m under a 2.1 m keel. Go round it.

q: You want a quiet night at anchor in this bay. Where do you drop the hook?
a: C — in the charted anchorage
o: A — beside the cable, in good mud
B — on the foul ground, closer in
D — by the pipeline, buried in sand
why: Never anchor over cables, pipelines or foul ground: the anchor snags or does damage. Use the charted anchorage.
ref: Chart symbols — anchorages, cables and pipelines

q: You must anchor here for the night with a blow forecast. Which spot gives your plough anchor the best holding?
a: C — sand and mud: it digs in
o: A — rock: it hooks under a ledge
B — weed: soft, so it buries
D — shells: hard, so it bites
why: Seabed on the chart: R rock, Wd weed, S sand, M mud, Sh shells. A plough holds best in sand and mud.
ref: Chart symbols — nature of the seabed

q: Your track rounds the headland through the area marked on the chart. What do you expect there now?
a: Steep, breaking seas — pass well outside
o: Smooth water — the stream flattens it
A helpful eddy close under the point
Shoal water, but only at LW springs
why: Overfalls: the stream runs over an uneven bottom. At springs with wind against tide the seas stand up and break.
ref: Chart symbols — overfalls and tide rips

q: Your planned shortcut crosses this area. What do you do?
a: Read Note B and keep out if it bans entry
o: Cross it — such areas are for ships only
Cross it at night, when nobody checks
Cross it fast, without stopping
why: The chart's note says what is prohibited — entry, anchoring or fishing. Obey it, and replan round if entry is banned.

fig.title: Chart extract
lines: A magenta pecked line encloses an area

q: Your track crosses the area marked on the chart, where the soundings read 11–12 m. What do you allow for?
a: Less water than charted — watch the depth
o: More water than charted — it is dredged
Strong eddies over the dumped ground
A ban on all small craft passing
why: A spoil ground is where dredged material is dumped: depths may be less than charted. Watch the sounder and don't anchor.

q: You run the charted measured mile both ways to check your speed under engine. What is your speed through the water at these revs?
a: 8.0 kn
o: 7.5 kn
6.0 kn
why: Average the speeds, not the times: 10.0 and 6.0 kn give 8.0 kn. The mean time, 8 min, would wrongly give 7.5 kn.

fig.title: Measured distance — 1852 m
lines: Run 1, with the stream: 6 min 00 s

q: You plan to cross the shipping lanes ahead. What is the tinted band between them?
a: The separation zone
o: An inshore traffic zone
A recommended track for yachts
A deep-water route
why: The tinted band between opposing lanes is the separation zone: cross it as part of a right-angle crossing, never linger.

q: What do 21m and 18/15M in this light's description tell you?
a: Light 21 m above MHWS; white 18 M, red 15 M
o: Tower 21 m tall; 18 M by day, 15 M by night
Light 21 m above LAT; red 18 M, white 15 M
21 m of water off it; range 18 to 15 M
why: Elevation is the light's height above the chart's height datum, here MHWS; nominal ranges are per colour, W then R.

q: You are approaching this sectored light at night. Which sector are you in?
a: White — sector arcs are from seaward
o: Red — sector arcs are from the light
Neither — the reversed 271° is dark
Both — the sector edges overlap
why: Sector limits are true bearings from seaward towards the light: a bearing of 091°T falls in W 085°–095°.

q: Fog closes in as you near this lighthouse. What do you listen for?
a: Two horn blasts every 30 seconds
o: One horn blast every 30 seconds
Two horn blasts every 3 minutes
One horn blast every 2 seconds
why: Horn(2) 30s: a group of two blasts, repeated every 30 seconds. Time the cycle to identify the station.

q: The shortcut passes close to the rocky shore, where there are no soundings inside the 10 m contour. What do you read into the blank?
a: Unsurveyed — rocks may be there
o: Deep water — no soundings needed
A flat bottom of exactly 10 m
Sand — soundings left out on sand
why: A blank inside a contour means no data, not deep water. Near a rocky shore assume dangers and keep to the sounded water.

q: Your crew points at the underlined figure in the middle of the bay and asks if you can sail over it at low water. What does it mean?
a: It dries 2.1 m above chart datum
o: 2.1 m of water over it at datum
21 m — the line marks a decimal
2.1 m more water than charted
why: An underlined sounding is a drying height: the bottom stands that far above chart datum and is dry at low water springs.

q: To reach the anchorage you must cross the drying bank on the chart. What height of tide do you need to keep your margin under the keel?
why: Height of tide needed = drying height + draft + margin = 2.3 + 1.8 + 0.5 = 4.6 m.

q: You are motoring up the river towards this bridge. What is the least clearance above your masthead you can ever have under it?
a: 1.5 m, at HAT — more at any lower tide
o: 1.5 m at chart datum — less at HW
18 m — the figure is the gap above you
None yet — add the height of tide first
why: Charted clearance is above HAT, the highest predicted tide: 18 − 16.5 = 1.5 m is the worst case; a lower tide adds to it.

q: You must pass under this bridge at tonight's high water. What margin will you have above the masthead?
why: Above MHWS the gap shrinks: 17.5 − 0.3 = 17.2 m, less 16.8 m = 0.4 m. Too tight for comfort if there is any swell.

fig.title: Bridge on an older chart
lines: Your air draft with antenna: 16.8 m

q: You are laying off courses on this chart this season. What variation do you use?
why: (9'E) is the annual change: 10 years × 9' = 1°30' eastward, so 4°10'W − 1°30' = 2°40'W.

q: Your crew lays the 245°M bearing straight off the rose's inner magnetic ring. How far out is the position line?
a: About 4° — the ring is set for 1998
o: None — the inner ring is always right
About 1° — variation changes slowly
About 5° — the whole old variation
why: 28 years × 8'E = 3°44', so variation is now 1°16'W, not 5°W: the 1998 inner ring is nearly 4° out.

fig.title: Compass rose on an old chart

q: You have applied this notice to your paper chart. How and where do you record it?
a: '2026-4512' in the bottom-left margin
o: Beside the edition date in the title
In the logbook only, not on the chart
In pencil by the nearest compass rose
why: Small corrections are logged in the chart's bottom-left margin by year and notice number, so the next user knows its state.
ref: Charts — corrections and Notices to Mariners

fig.title: Chart correction
lines: You have just inked it in

q: Before the season you check this chart against the Notices to Mariners. Which do you apply?
o: All three, in number order
2026-0412 only, this year's notice
why: Apply every notice after the last one recorded: 2988 is older than 3120 and already in; apply 3305, then 0412.
ref: Charts — corrections and Notices to Mariners

fig.title: Bringing a chart up to date

q: How do you put this temporary notice on your paper chart?
a: In pencil, rubbed out when it is cancelled
o: In ink, like a permanent correction
Not at all — temporary notices lapse
In the margin only, not on the chart
why: Temporary and Preliminary (T&P) notices go on in pencil and come off when the notice is cancelled or made permanent.
ref: Charts — corrections and Notices to Mariners

fig.title: Notice to Mariners (T)
lines: East cardinal buoy off the reef

q: The leg looks clear on the plotter but not on the paper chart. Why?
a: Vector charts drop detail when zoomed out
o: A recent update removed the rock
Plotters show only lit dangers
Raster charts never show single rocks
why: A vector chart shows features by zoom level and display settings. Check every leg zoomed in, or with the route check.

fig.title: Plotter, vector chart
lines: Zoomed out to see the whole leg
Paper chart: an isolated rock on the leg

q: Your mate says 15 m is plenty, because the screen shows the rock so clearly. What do you say?
a: Overscale magnifies the errors — give it room
o: Agree — zooming in makes the chart more exact
Agree — as long as GPS has four satellites
Agree — the raster image is the paper chart
why: Zooming past the chart's scale enlarges its errors, not its accuracy; at ×8 on an old survey, 15 m means nothing.

fig.title: Plotter at the harbour approach
lines: Approach chart from an old survey
Route drawn 15 m off a rock

q: You are checking this route in your passage plan. Is the clearance off the patch enough?
a: No — 0.15 M is inside the position error
o: Yes — 0.15 M is more than a cable
Yes — the patch is deeper than the keel
Yes — GPS puts you within 10 m
why: 0.15 M ≈ 280 m, well inside ZOC C's ±500 m: the patch could be under you. Pass at least 0.3 M off and watch the depth.

fig.title: Vector chart, data quality
lines: Route: 0.15 M off a 3.0 m patch

q: You are feeling your way into this cove. How far do you trust the charted soundings and rocks?
a: Little — a poor survey; go slow on the sounder
o: Fully — two stars is a top rating
Fully for depth; positions may be 5 m out
Fully — the stars mark a recent survey
why: Two stars is ZOC D, worse than C: positions and depths are poor and rocks may be missing. Go slowly, sound and look.

fig.title: Plotter, vector chart
lines: Soundings 4–6 m, a few rocks shown

q: Your plotter has died on a night passage. What gives you your position now?
a: A DR from the 0100 fix on the paper chart
o: Waiting for the plotter to reboot
Closing the coast to fix on a light
Asking the coastguard for a position
why: This is why you keep a paper plot: the 0100 fix and the log give you a DR or EP at once.

fig.title: 0200, 12 M offshore
lines: Paper chart: last fix plotted at 0100
Log written up hourly: course, log

q: Tomorrow you leave a standard port. You need the time and height of HW, the harbour office's VHF channel and the coastguard's weather broadcast times. Which single book do you open?
a: This year's nautical almanac
o: The pilot book for the coast
The List of Lights
The chart symbols booklet
why: The almanac holds the year's tide tables, tidal stream data, lights, radio data and port information in one book.

q: You are entering this harbour for the first time. How do you use the pilot book's plan?
a: With the chart — as a guide to it
o: Instead of the chart — it is newer
Not at all — it is not allowed
By day only, never at night
why: Pilot book plans are sketches for orientation — berths, facilities, the approach. Navigate on the official chart.

fig.title: Pilot book, harbour plan
lines: Plan shows the berths and the approach
Printed under it: 'Not to be used

q: You are writing up the lights for a night arrival. Where do you find the full detail of this light?
a: The List of Lights and Fog Signals
o: The List of Radio Signals
The chart symbols booklet
The tidal stream atlas
why: The List of Lights gives each light's full description: sectors, phases, fog signal, structure and elevation.

fig.title: Lighthouse on the chart
lines: You need its sector limits, its fog
signal and how it looks by day

q: You will arrive at this port tomorrow. Which publication sets all of this out in full?
a: The List of Radio Signals
o: The List of Lights and Fog Signals
The tidal stream atlas
The chart symbols booklet
why: The List of Radio Signals covers coast radio, safety broadcasts, VTS and port operations: channels, times, reporting points.

fig.title: Arriving at a big commercial port
lines: and the times of safety broadcasts

q: You are planning to round a big headland and want to see the direction and rate of the stream across the whole area, hour by hour. What do you open?
a: The tidal stream atlas
o: The tide tables
The List of Lights
The pilot book's harbour plans
why: A tidal stream atlas shows the streams over the area for each hour before and after HW at its reference port.

q: On a newly bought chart you meet a symbol and an abbreviation you have never seen, close to your track. Where do you look them up?
a: Chart 5011, Symbols and Abbreviations
o: The List of Lights
The pilot book's glossary
The weekly Notices to Mariners
why: Admiralty chart 5011 (the INT 1 symbols) explains every symbol and abbreviation used on the charts.

q: Which set of charts and publications do you carry for this passage?
a: Passage chart, charts of all four ports, almanac, pilot
o: Passage chart and almanac; the plotter has the ports
Charts of departure and destination; old almanac
Plotter charts, a pilot book and the radio list
why: Carry paper charts of the route and of every port you may use, this year's almanac and a pilot book; the plotter is extra.

fig.title: Coastal passage, 48 M, overnight
lines: two ports of refuge on the way

q: You are passing this rock off the Brittany coast near low water. How high above the sea does it stand now?
why: (3) is a height above MHWS: 3 + 5.2 = 8.2 m above datum. The sea is 0.8 m above datum, so 8.2 − 0.8 = 7.4 m.

fig.note: Heights above MHWS, depths below CD

q: Your crew says you will see the rock on the chart and steer round it by eye. When can you expect to see it?
a: Only near LW — now 3.1 m of water covers it
o: Now — awash means it is at the surface
At HW, when the sea breaks over it
Never — it lies 3.1 m below datum
why: Awash at chart datum: it shows only when the tide is near datum. With 3.1 m of tide it is 3.1 m down — steer by a clearing line.

q: Your track passes over this wreck. How much water will you have under the keel at least?
why: Swept to 4.2 m: nothing on it is shallower. 4.2 + 0.5 m of tide = 4.7 m of water, less the 2.0 m draft = 2.7 m.

q: Your shortcut crosses the shoal patch on the chart, in a long Atlantic swell. What do you do?
a: Go round it — the swell may break there
o: Cross — 1.8 m under the keel is ample
Cross fast, so you are over it briefly
Cross — swell only matters off a beach
why: 3.4 + 0.6 = 4.0 m, but a trough of a 2.5 m swell leaves about 2.75 m, and seas can break on the patch. Keep off it.

q: Your planned track passes 2 cables south of the rock on the chart. What do you do?
a: Give it a much wider berth
o: Keep the track — 2 cables is ample
Keep the track — PA means it is marked
Keep the track, but only by day
why: PA — position approximate: the rock was never fixed accurately and may lie some way from its symbol. Allow a wide margin.

q: Your crew suggests sailing straight over the rock, since it may not exist. What do you do?
a: Treat it as real and go round
o: Sail over it — ED means it is gone
Sail over it, but only at high water
Sail over it slowly, watching the depth
why: ED — existence doubtful: reported but never confirmed. Doubtful is not absent: plan as if the rock is there.

q: The main light is already in sight. Your mate is now looking for this pierhead light, still 12 M off. When do you expect to see it?
a: Within about 3 M of it
o: Now — clear nights show every light
Within about 6 M — its elevation
At about 12 M, with the main light
why: 3M is the nominal range: in clear weather this light carries only about 3 M. 6m is its height above MHWS, not its range.

q: You are closing the coast at night, expecting to pick up this light. What do you see?
a: Nothing — on 230°T it is obscured
o: The light — you are within its range
A red sector warning you off the land
Only its loom, as it stands 30 m high
why: Obscd 210°–245°: on those bearings from seaward land hides the light. You will not see it until the bearing leaves that arc.

q: You are 20 M offshore heading in on a clear night. Which light do you see first, and at about what range?
a: B, at about 16 M
o: A, at about 22 M
B, at about 19 M
A, at about 11 M
why: B clears the horizon at 2.08(√60 + √2) ≈ 19 M but its nominal range is 16 M; A rises only at ≈ 11 M. Take the lesser limit.

q: On a hazy night you watch for this buoy on the radar. What does the chart tell you to look for?
a: A Morse T painted just beyond its echo
o: A white light flashing T in Morse
An AIS target named T on the plotter
A fog signal sounding T in Morse
why: A racon answers your radar: it paints its Morse letter — here T, one dash — on the screen just beyond the mark's echo.

q: At dawn you reach the position in the notice and see no buoy at all. What do you make of it?
a: Normal — the mark exists only on AIS
o: The buoy has broken adrift — report it
Your GPS is off — you are lost
The wreck has been cleared away
why: A virtual AIS aid is a signal, not a buoy: it shows only on AIS and the plotter. Treat it as an east cardinal and pass east.
ref: Chart symbols — AIS aids to navigation

fig.title: Notice to Mariners
lines: Marked by a virtual AIS aid (V-AIS):
east cardinal; no buoy laid yet

q: You are approaching this mark on the chart. Which side do you pass it?
a: East of it
o: West of it
North of it
Either side, keeping close
why: BYB with Q(3) 10s is an east cardinal: the safe water lies to the east of the mark.

q: You arrive late in this crowded bay and want a buoy for the night. Which do you pick up?
a: B — a visitors' mooring
o: A — any free private buoy
C — the fish farm's corner buoy
D — the big buoy by the fairway
why: The chart marks visitors' moorings for passing yachts. Private buoys have owners, and fairway or fish-farm buoys are not moorings.

q: You need diesel for tomorrow's leg. What is your plan on arrival?
a: Berth on C tonight, fuel after 0800
o: Go straight to the fuel berth at 2130
Lie on the fuel berth overnight
Skip the call and take any free berth
why: The page gives the fuel hours: shut at 2130. Call on Ch 37, take a visitors' berth on C and fuel when it opens at 0800.

fig.title: Almanac — marina page
lines: Visitors: pontoon C; call Ch 37 first

q: You want to stop in this Croatian cove for the night. What do you do?
a: Pick up a reserve buoy; do not anchor
o: Anchor in the weed — it holds well
Anchor on the sand patch in 10 m
Anchor after dark and leave at dawn
why: The chart's note bans anchoring inside the reserve to protect the seagrass. Use its mooring buoys or anchor outside the line.

fig.note: Note D: no anchoring; visitor buoys

q: On this chart of the Norwegian coast your GPS reads 60°23.5'N 005°01.0'E. Which mark is the boat?
a: C
o: A
B
D
why: At 60°N a minute of longitude is drawn half as long as a minute of latitude. 1.0' east of 5°00'E and 0.5' south of 60°24'N meet at C.

fig.note: Parallels and meridians from the border

q: You are motoring east along the Norwegian coast on this leg. When do you reach the waypoint?
You check the plotter's figures for this leg against the chart. What course and distance do you lay off?
Both fixes lie on the same meridian. How far have you made good to the north between them?
why: From 49°58.6' up to 50°00' is 1.4', then 3.1' more: 4.5' of latitude = 4.5 M. Count across the degree line.

q: You have walked the parallel rule from your leg to the rose. What do you write in the passage plan?
why: The outer ring of a chart rose is true and the inner ring magnetic. A °T column takes the outer reading: 062°T.

fig.title: Laying off the course
lines: Parallel rule walked to the rose

q: You check the 0300 EP against the charted rocks. How far apart are they on the paper?
a: About 2 mm
o: About 2 cm
About 0.2 mm
About 9 mm
why: 0.5 M = 926 m; 926 m ÷ 500,000 = 1.9 mm, about a pencil dot. Near danger, plot on a larger-scale chart.

fig.title: Passage chart, 0300
lines: Charted rocks 0.5 M from the EP

q: What do you make of your mate's 2 cables?
a: Too fine — the dot alone is 3 cables
o: Right — a dot is plotted to 10 m
Too coarse — it is nearer 2 M
Right — the scale does not matter
why: 1.5 mm × 350,000 = 525 m, nearly 3 cables: on this scale a 2-cable offset is lost inside the dot itself.

fig.title: Night, passage chart
lines: EP drawn as a dot 1.5 mm across

q: The helm loses night vision every time you look at the plotter. What do you change?
a: Switch to the vector chart's night colours
o: Turn the raster up bright for contrast
Switch the plotter off for the night
Keep the raster but zoom right out
why: A vector chart redraws itself in a dark night palette; a raster is a picture of the paper chart and can only be dimmed or tinted.

fig.title: Night passage, chart table
lines: the white paper glares into the cockpit

q: You need this light's characteristic and sectors from the plotter. How do you get them?
a: Tap it to query the object's details
o: Rotate the chart to north-up
Switch the plotter to night colours
Nothing — vectors hold no light data

Fine — the tide always adds water

Cross: 3.5 m of water, 1.4 m spare

Ink it in and log 2025-3982 again
Apply it in pencil until next year
why: Each notice names the one before it for that chart. Yours stops at 3982, so 4410 is missing: apply it, then 1120.

Ignore it — the buoy will show you
Pass over it — 2.6 m is deep enough

The coastguard on Ch 16
Nobody — just go in quietly

By the plotter's position, as shown

Fine — 0.2 m is a fair margin
why: Depths from mean sea level leave nothing in hand: a small tide and high pressure (about 1 cm per hPa) can drop the sea 0.2–0.3 m.

q: You are cruising the Cyclades with this chart. What variation goes into your courses this year?
why: 8 years × 6'E = 48' more east: 4°20'E + 0°48' = 5°08'E. An easterly change adds to an easterly variation.
